name: Sam Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing biomedical science, so it's cell biology, chemistry and a lot of lab practicals. A normal week is lectures in the morning, lab on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons, and in the evenings I'm usually messing about with a study tool I built. It takes my lecture slides and quizzes me on them. I live in a flat share with a guy doing maths and a girl doing music, and my parents in Linz send a monthly transfer that covers everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it's still useful. I'd tell my friends that even if it's hype, a lot of small things become easy, and the people who learn the tools now will have an edge. I'd post my study tool on the course forum and say try it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I find this stuff exciting. I like the idea of AI finding new drugs and it being a big deal. But I'd also be fine, because my degree is solid either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd keep building tools for my own studying, keep my AI use daily, and maybe pitch the study tool to a few classmates for a small fee. I'd also apply for the summer research placement at the university's cancer lab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and slightly bored. Nothing scary is happening, and my money is sorted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd charge classmates for the study tool. What made you think of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My flatmate Lena asked if she could use it for her music theory exams, and she said she'd pay five euros a month. It made me realise it doesn't take much to turn a small thing into a bit of income. I won't get rich, but it's a good habit for later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever worry that relying on AI every day makes you lazy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes. I try to do the hard bit myself first, then ask the tool to check me, not the other way round. My tutor said that people who only copy answers will crash in the exam. So I treat it like a very fast study partner and I still do the work.

say: I'd say it's still **useful**, and learning the tools now gives people an edge.
I'd post my study tool on the course forum and tell people to **try it**.
think: Privately I'm a bit **disappointed**, because I find AI drug discovery exciting.
I know my degree is **solid** either way.
do: Keep building **study tools** and pitch one to classmates for a small fee.
Apply for the summer **cancer lab** placement.
feel: I feel **calm** and slightly bored, with money sorted.
S0.quote: I try to do the hard bit myself first, then ask the tool to check me, not the other way round
fieldNote: He treats AI as a **study partner** and is aware of the laziness risk, which shows maturity.
The small **side income** idea came from his flatmate Lena, a music student, not from a plan.
Money is secure, so even a hyped-down world feels **calm**, a little flat for someone who finds change exciting.

steps.text: Keep building and refining my own study tool
Offer the quiz tool to classmates for five euros a month
Apply for the summer cancer lab placement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, finally, but people have to get ready. The thinking tasks go first, so anyone who just passes information along is in trouble. I'd say it online and in classes, but also tell people to try the tools themselves and not just worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my field is mixed. Lab work with pipettes stays human for a while, but a lot of analysis, reading papers and writing reports will shift to software. So a graduate who can use AI to run experiments and analyse data is more valuable, and someone who can't is not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn Python properly and some bioinformatics, so I can work with AI on research data. I'd build a small project, like a tool that scans papers for a certain protein. And I'd try to get a summer placement in a lab that is already using machine learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and uneasy together. It's an opportunity for me, but I know not everyone on my course will move as fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not everyone on your course will keep up. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lab partner Ravi, who still prints every paper and writes notes by hand. He's smart, but he doesn't like new tools, and when I show him a shortcut he says he'll do it his way. I worry that in three years he'll find the entry-level jobs have changed and he hasn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a fair response look like from the university or government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Free short courses for everyone on how to use these tools, taught properly. Not just for the keen people like me. If the university doesn't do it, the gap between students like me and students who still print every paper will grow, and that's an unfair advantage I didn't earn.

say: I'd say **thinking tasks** go first, so people who only pass information along are in trouble.
I'd tell people to **try the tools** themselves instead of just worrying.
think: I think graduates who can use AI on research data become **more valuable**.
Lab bench work stays human for now, but **analysis and reports** shift to software.
do: Learn **Python and bioinformatics** to work with AI on research data.
Build a small project that scans papers for a certain **protein**.
feel: I feel **excited and uneasy**, because not everyone will keep up.
S1.quote: the gap between students like me and students who still print every paper will grow, and that's an unfair advantage I didn't earn
fieldNote: He sees himself as a **winner** in this change and feels a bit guilty about it.
Lab partner Ravi, who prints every paper, is his example of someone who may be **left behind**.
His unease is about **fairness**, not about his own job.

steps.text: Learn Python and bioinformatics through an online course
Build a tool that scans papers for one protein
Ask the university for free short AI courses for all students

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this changes everything and we need emergency rules now. I'd say governments should tax the AI companies and set up a basic income. I'd tell people not to wait for adults to sort it out, and to start using the tools while they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be worried but also energised. By 2028 I'm in my second year, and the full AGI could do the analysis and reading I'm trained for. My job would be to stand where the machine can't, like the lab and clinical side, for maybe three more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw myself into it. I'd learn every tool I can, build projects, and try to get into a lab that works with AI. I'd also save my allowance, because I've never done that, and ask my parents to keep their savings safe. And I'd join a campaign for a basic income pilot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with adrenaline. It's like standing at the top of a ski run when you're not sure of the snow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the ski run feel like in your body, when you picture it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My stomach drops a bit, and then I want to get moving. I'd be checking the news every day and talking to my dad, who is a civil engineer in Linz and would be exposed himself. I'd hate having no say in how fast it happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents in that situation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad to move into something that involves site visits and people, not just drawings, because drawings will go first. I'd tell my mum, who is a pharmacist, that she's safer, but should learn the new tools. And I'd say they can stop sending me money if they need it, because I'd work.

say: I'd say governments should **tax AI companies** and run a basic income now.
I'd tell people not to wait for adults and to **use the tools** while they can.
think: I'm worried but **energised**, since AGI could do the analysis I'm trained for.
I'd aim to stand where the machine can't: the **lab** and clinical side.
do: Learn **every tool**, build projects and aim for a lab working with AI.
Back a **basic income** pilot and save my allowance, which I've never done.
feel: I feel **anxious** with adrenaline, like standing at the top of a ski run.
S2.quote: I'd tell my dad to move into something that involves site visits and people, not just drawings, because drawings will go first
fieldNote: His worry is about **family earners**, especially his father, a civil engineer, rather than himself.
Adaptive instinct is to **move first**: tools, projects, a lab that uses AI.
He'd offer to give up his **allowance** and earn instead, which shows how real the threat feels.

steps.text: Learn every AI research tool and build a portfolio project
Join the basic income pilot campaign
Save part of my allowance each month
Tell Dad to move toward site visits and people work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to turn it into something good, if we move now. I'd tell my course group to get skills in both science and AI, and to talk to politicians. I'd say we shouldn't let a few companies decide who benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years means I graduate in 2029 and then work for two years before AGI is complete in 2031. Hands-on lab work should be there a bit longer, until 2034. So I'd want to be the person who runs experiments with AI, not someone who competes with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the degree, learn Python and machine learning in my spare time, and try for a placement in a lab that uses AI. I'd save the allowance and any job money. And I'd get involved in a student group that talks about AI policy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed, mostly hopeful. I'm uneasy about the end point, but five years gives me time to be good at something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want to run experiments with AI. What does that look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I imagine designing the question, setting up the experiment, and letting the AI analyse hundreds of results while I check the odd ones. My lab placement last summer was like that in a small way, with a professor who used a tool to sort cell images. It saved days, and I could see exactly where it was wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up for those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably social time and a year abroad. I'd rather stay and build skills than do an exchange in Spain. It's a trade I'd make, though I'd feel a bit boring. My girlfriend isn't happy about it, and we've talked it through.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** if we move now, and companies shouldn't decide who benefits.
I'd tell my course group to get skills in **science and AI**.
think: I'd graduate in 2029, work two years, and want to **run experiments with AI**.
I'd rather not compete with the machine, so I'd learn to **direct** it.
do: Learn **machine learning** in my spare time and seek an AI-using lab placement.
Give up a **year abroad** to stay and build skills.
feel: I feel **hopeful** but uneasy about the end point.
S3.quote: I imagine designing the question, setting up the experiment, and letting the AI analyse hundreds of results while I check the odd ones
fieldNote: Time lets him build a concrete picture of his future role: **direction** over competition.
He has a **real lab example** of AI saving days of work.
His trade-off, skipping a year abroad, shows he treats the **timeline** seriously, though his girlfriend disagrees.

steps.text: Learn machine learning in spare evenings
Apply for a lab placement that uses AI
Join a student group on AI policy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and we should use it well. I'd say, do the degree, but also learn how to build with the tools, and push for fair laws. I'd probably post a lot about it and annoy my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a bit thrilled. A decade is a PhD and a few years of research. I could be working on real drug discovery when AGI is complete, and then maybe I'm the one using it to do it faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the degree, apply for a master's and then a PhD in computational biology. I'd keep building tools and try to publish something. And I'd stay involved in the policy side, because I'd like to see rules in place by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and excited. It's the best version for me, because I have time to become useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different about your choices when you have ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can aim for a PhD without worrying that the whole field will be automated before I finish. With two years I'd rush into anything, with ten I can learn the basics properly first. I'd also take a proper break in the summers, because I'm usually going at full speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the downside of ten years for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The risk is that I get complacent, and that the people with less time or money fall behind quietly. I'm lucky, because my parents pay for everything, and I can plan around a long timeline. A single mum working two jobs can't plan around a long timeline like that, and I'd want the system to remember her.

say: I'd say ten years is long, so **use it well** and push for fair laws.
I'd tell friends to study the degree and also learn to **build with the tools**.
think: I'm **thrilled**: a decade covers a PhD and real drug discovery research.
I'd love to be the one using AGI to find drugs **faster**.
do: Aim for a **PhD** in computational biology after the master's.
Keep building tools and try to **publish** something.
feel: I feel **calm and excited**, with time to become useful.
S4.quote: A single mum working two jobs can't plan around a long timeline like that, and I'd want the system to remember her
fieldNote: Time makes his optimism fully **concrete**: master's, PhD, publication.
He names his **privilege** without being asked, and links it to fairness.
The only downside he sees is **complacency** and others falling behind.

steps.text: Apply for a master's in computational biology
Publish a small research tool with a supervisor
Stay involved in student AI policy groups

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it's too fast for my parents and for people who can't move quickly. I'd be fine, but my dad's drawing work would go first. What would help is free training for everyone, a basic income and rules that make the companies share what they earn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not naive about my situation. I'm excited because I'm well off and adaptable, and not everyone is. If I'm going to be a scientist who uses this, I want to be one who also pushes for fair rules.

headlineQuote: I'm excited because I'm well off and adaptable, and not everyone is
portrait: Sam is a 19-year-old **biomedical science** student from Linz whose parents cover all costs.
He uses **AI daily**, builds his own study tools and treats the tool as a partner, not a crutch.
Progressive, he links his own advantage to **fairness** and backs a basic income and free training.
His mood is calm when time is long and **anxious** at 2028, mainly for his father's engineering job.
He moves first: Python, machine learning, lab placements and a plan for a PhD.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** most, because his parents and less mobile people can't adapt in time.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **free training** for everyone, a basic income and rules that make companies share the gains.
